title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 20: ABS-CBN v. Comelec: Exit Polls — a New Paradigm of Free Expression
primary_topics: Chapter 20 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's account of ABS-CBN v. Comelec, in which his ponencia held that exit polls are a species of free expression entitled to constitutional protection and that the Comelec could not totally ban them.

His framing of free expression as an ever-expanding frontier that has grown with technology, from medieval free speech and assembly through the printing press, labor picketing, radio and television, and now toward the Internet, broadband fiber optics and teleconferencing.

The doctrinal core of the Decision: free expression is a 'preferred' right, prior restraint is presumed invalid, the 'clear and present danger' test governs, and a restriction must serve a substantial government interest by the least restrictive means.

His rejection of the Comelec's arguments as 'purely speculative and clearly untenable,' coupled with an offer of narrowly tailored alternatives to a total ban, and his answer to the dissents of Justices Vitug and Kapunan, including the question of mootness.
sub_topics: He opens with a history of expanding expression -- free speech and peaceful assembly in the Middle Ages, freedom of the press after the printing press, the right to strike and picket in the Industrial Age, then radio and television -- and predicts that the Internet and teleconferencing will follow.
The question presented: could the Comelec, in the guise of protecting the sanctity of elections and the secrecy of the ballot, totally prohibit exit polls and the dissemination of their results?
His unequivocal answer of 'No,' in a ponencia concurred in by the Chief Justice and eight other justices.

The Court's definition of exit polls as a species of electoral survey confidentially asking randomly selected voters whom they voted for immediately after casting their ballots, first used in the May 11, 1998 elections.

The nature and scope of free expression: a 'preferred' right standing higher than substantive economic liberties, the liberty to discuss publicly and truthfully any matter of public interest without prior restraint, and a commitment to debate that is 'uninhibited, robust, and wide open.'

Limitations acknowledged: while the liberty to think is absolute, expression is subject to police power, and Cabansag v. Fernandez's two tests -- 'clear and present danger' and 'dangerous tendency' -- are contrasted, with the Court adhering to the former.

The justification standard: the power of prior restraint is not presumed, the presumption is against its validity, the respondent bears the burden, and the restriction must further a substantial governmental interest unrelated to suppressing expression by means no greater than essential.

The Comelec's contentions rebutted: randomness is the nature of a survey, the results do not replace the official count, and the credibility of elections is not at stake since an exit poll is only part of the electoral exercise.
Overbreadth: the Resolution applied without qualification as to whether polling was disruptive, and no evidence showed that exit polls or poll reporters cause chaos or confuse voters near precincts.

The research cost of a ban: valuable data on voting behavior and the impact of current events would remain unknown and unexplored, citing Daily Herald Co. v. Munro on insulating voters from outside influences.

The less restrictive alternatives he listed: designated areas, only professional survey groups, a reasonable distance from voting centers, notice that interviews are voluntary and unofficial, distinctive clothing, an information campaign, and a general prohibition of disruptive behavior.

ABS-CBN's own methodology: random selection of communities and residences, interviews only of voters with indelible ink on their fingers, no cameras, and release of results only the day after the elections.

The ballot secrecy argument answered: the ban's premise is off-tangent because the petitioner sought no access to ballots, the principle exists to prevent vote buying through voter identification, and a voter's verbal, voluntary disclosure exposes no ballot.

The dissents: Justice Vitug, joined by Justices Melo and Mendoza, would have dismissed the petition as technically moot and declined a preemptive judgment; Justice Kapunan agreed on mootness, rejected the presumption of invalidity given the Comelec's constitutional mandate, and warned that snail-paced counting and special elections could make 'trending' and the 'bandwagon-effect' real.

His resolution of mootness: the implications on the people's fundamental freedom transcend the past election, and under Salonga v. Cruz Pano the Court has a symbolic function of educating bench and bar.
His concluding satisfaction with the 10-4 vote, with one abstention, as proof that the Court can meet head-on new paradigms of free expression created by science and technology.

stances.claim: Exit polls are a new species of free expression entitled to constitutional protection, so the Comelec may not totally prohibit them or the dissemination of their results.
stances.rhetorical_move: historical expansion argument -- each new medium has been brought under the constitutional mantle -- followed by an unequivocal answer in the negative to the Comelec's power

stances.claim: The Comelec's fears that exit polls sow confusion and destroy the credibility of the electoral process are purely speculative and clearly untenable, and the total ban is too broad because it applies without regard to whether the polling is actually disruptive.
stances.rhetorical_move: point-by-point refutation plus an overbreadth and least-restrictive-means analysis

stances.claim: Exit polls do not violate ballot secrecy, because the principle exists to prevent vote buying through voter identification and a voter's voluntary verbal disclosure exposes no ballot.
stances.rhetorical_move: purpose-of-the-rule reasoning that recharacterizes the objection as off-tangent

stances.claim: The freedom to hold exit polls remains subject to reasonable regulation, and narrowly tailored counter-measures may be prescribed to minimize incidental problems without transgressing fundamental rights.
stances.rhetorical_move: self-qualification that concedes regulatory space while preserving the right

stances.claim: Justice Kapunan argued that the Comelec's constitutional mandate displaces any presumption of invalidity and that, given the country's snail-paced counting and special elections, exit poll results could still produce trending and disruption.
stances.rhetorical_move: reproduction of the dissenting position in its own words

notable_anecdotes: CJP recalls writing the ponencia and answering the question 'with an unequivocal "No"' for a majority that included the Chief Justice and eight other justices.
He recounts that exit polls had never been resorted to in Philippine electoral history until the May 11, 1998 elections -- the very elections the Comelec Resolution covered.
He describes listing concrete alternatives to a ban, down to requiring pollsters to wear distinctive clothing so voters would not mistake them for election officials.
He reproduces ABS-CBN's own methodology, including interviewing only voters with indelible ink on their fingers and using no cameras of any sort.

He ends by saying he is 'quite happy with the Court's Decision,' carried 10-4 with one abstention, and expects the Court to meet the constitutional questions posed by the Internet and teleconferencing.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 20 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounts ABS-CBN v. Comelec, the exit poll case. CJP opens with a history of free expression widening alongside technology -- from free speech and peaceful assembly in the Middle Ages, to freedom of the press after the printing press, to labor's right to strike and picket, to radio and television -- and predicts that the Internet, broadband fiber optics and teleconferencing will raise the same questions. The issue was whether the Comelec, invoking the sanctity of elections and the secrecy of the ballot, could totally prohibit exit polls and the publication of their results. Writing for a majority that included the Chief Justice and eight other justices, he answered no. The Decision defined exit polls as a species of electoral survey confidentially asking randomly selected voters whom they had voted for immediately after balloting, first used in the May 11, 1998 elections. It restated free expression as a 'preferred' right, held that prior restraint is presumed invalid and that the restrainer bears the burden, adhered to the clear and present danger test over the dangerous tendency test, and required any restriction to serve a substantial governmental interest by means no greater than essential. He dismissed the Comelec's fears as purely speculative, noted that a survey is random by nature and does not replace the official count, found the Resolution overbroad for applying without regard to actual disruption, and observed that a ban would also foreclose long-term research into voting behavior. In place of prohibition he listed narrowly tailored measures -- designated areas, professional pollsters kept at a distance, voluntary interviews, distinctive clothing, an information campaign. He answered the ballot secrecy objection by tracing the rule to the prevention of vote buying, and answered the dissents of Justices Vitug and Kapunan, including their mootness point, by invoking the Court's duty under Salonga v. Cruz Pano to educate bench and bar. The Decision carried 10-4 with one abstention.
